plays.counter: Ragnar should never have let one person control both his supply and his secret. For Yidu, the lesson is to hold leverage quietly and never threaten a party who can remove you more cheaply than he can comply.
plays.principle: Leverage without protection is a death warrant: the moment you threaten, you become the problem to solve.
plays.in_practice: Being a client's single supplier of something critical gives you negotiating power, but using it as a threat usually ends the relationship. Use it to earn a better seat, then keep delivering value.

quote.text: It's the only way you can get your medicine. And you may need me for other things as well.
quote.speaker: Yidu

plays.title: The Blacksmith's Daughter
plays.target: The blacksmith who forged the ship's anchor
plays.context: Ragnar is secretly building a ship to raid west against the orders of Earl Haraldson, the local ruler. The blacksmith knows about it because he forged the anchor, and if he tells the Earl the voyage is exposed.
plays.play: Floki, the eccentric shipbuilder, takes a lock of hair from the blacksmith's daughter and promises to kill her if the blacksmith goes to Haraldson. The blacksmith delivers the anchor. Then Haraldson and his enforcer Svein visit the forge. The blacksmith denies everything until Svein seizes his daughter, at which point he confesses. Haraldson promises the girl will not be harmed and kills the blacksmith instead.
plays.why_it_works: It fails. Leverage through a person's family holds only while you are the most credible threat in the room, and Haraldson has more power and is physically present, so his threat overrides Floki's distant one.
plays.outcome: The Earl confirms the ship exists, though he decides the crew will die at sea anyway. The blacksmith pays with his life for being caught between two threats.
plays.counter: Floki needed a secret that a stronger party could not extract. Secrecy protected by fear is only as good as the fear, so the better plan was to keep the blacksmith ignorant of the ship's purpose.
plays.principle: Leverage held by fear fails the moment someone more frightening arrives.
plays.in_practice: Confidentiality that rests on a supplier's goodwill or a threat will not survive pressure from a bigger customer. Protect sensitive plans by limiting who knows, not by relying on promises.

quote.text: I promised him that if he went to Earl Haraldson I would find a way to kill her.
quote.speaker: Floki

plays.title: The Hostage That Backfired
plays.target: Hvitserk, his brother
plays.context: Ivar now rules Kattegat and claims to be a god. His brother Hvitserk openly doubts it and is in love with Thora, whose family has criticized Ivar. Ivar wants Hvitserk out of the city and needs an envoy to King Olaf of Norway.
plays.play: Ivar tells Hvitserk that he loves him and worries about his idle life, and offers him the post of envoy to Olaf. When Hvitserk refuses, Ivar introduces himself to Thora and remarks that it would be a pity if he had to burn her alive. Hvitserk agrees to leave at dawn. While he is away, Ivar burns Thora anyway.
plays.why_it_works: Threatening what someone loves buys instant compliance. It fails because Ivar sends a resentful man to his most important ally, and then kills the hostage, leaving his envoy with nothing left to protect.
plays.outcome: Hvitserk asks Olaf to attack Ivar instead of joining him, and Olaf eventually agrees. Hvitserk throws in with Ivar's enemies, and their armies combine at Kattegat.
plays.counter: The counter was Ivar's own to make: never make a man you have coerced your ambassador, and never destroy the hostage that is your only hold on him.
plays.principle: Never send someone you have coerced to represent you; they will negotiate against you.
plays.in_practice: Do not put an unhappy or pressured employee in charge of your most important client relationship. Their resentment will reach the client, and they may leave and take the client with them.

quote.text: Then it would be a pity if I had to burn her alive.
quote.speaker: Ivar
